blocks.text: Ecclesiastes 11 holds together two truths about human existence: people must act decisively in the world despite their fundamental ignorance about outcomes, and they must embrace life's joys while remaining aware of mortality and judgment. The chapter combines practical urgings to sow, give, and work with clear-eyed acknowledgment that humans cannot control results or fully understand God's purposes. Within this framework of human limitation and divine inscrutability, the passage goes on to commend enjoyment as a real and legitimate good.

The opening verses command generous action despite unpredictability: 'Cast thy bread upon the waters; for thou shalt find it after many days' and 'Give a portion to seven, yea, even unto eight.' Verses 3-6 explore this through natural imagery and observation. Rain falls where the clouds release it; trees fall in whatever direction they lean; the wind's path cannot be predicted. The farmer does not and cannot know in advance which of his seeds will succeed or whether both will prosper equally, yet he is commanded to sow in morning and evening, withholding nothing. Verse 5 makes the principle explicit: just as humans cannot comprehend how bones grow within the womb or how the wind moves, 'even so thou knowest not the work of God who doeth all.' This unknowing is not meant to paralyze but to clarify the boundary between human and divine action. People act; God accomplishes.

Despite this radical uncertainty, verses 7-10 pivot to commend a kind of joyful living. 'Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun. Yea, if a man live many years, let him rejoice in them all.' A young man is urged to celebrate his youth: 'let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart, and in the sight of thine eyes.' These are not commands to escape or indulge recklessly; rather, they present rejoicing and the appreciation of life's goodness as a real good that can be embraced. Yet the passage immediately qualifies this: remember 'the days of darkness, for they shall be many.' Furthermore, 'know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.' Joy and light exist as gifts within time, yet time itself is ultimately vanity (something transient and insubstantial). Judgment awaits. Still, the passage affirms that while we live, we may and should rejoice.
